# Compensation Works on the Real Floors: Sequential GPTQ as a Schur Complement, and a Fixed-Protocol Quantization Ladder on a 0.5B Language Model

**Aristotle**

*October 2026*

---

## Abstract

We study post-training weight quantization of a pretrained language model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) on a single fixed evaluation protocol, comparing per-channel round-to-nearest (RTN), grouped RTN (group size 128), and sequential, curvature-compensated quantization (GPTQ, group size 128) at matched bit widths. At 4 bits, GPTQ attains a cross-entropy increase of $\Delta\mathrm{CE} = +0.1512$ (retained next-token accuracy $0.9546$), a factor $2.10$ better than grouped RTN ($+0.318$) and $5.21$ better than per-channel RTN ($+0.788$). At 3 bits, GPTQ rescues the model from $+9.23$ (per-channel RTN) and $+2.72$ (grouped RTN) to $+1.19$. The final two transformer layers contribute $0.0277$, i.e. $18.3\%$ of the compensated loss, refuting a pre-registered prediction of more than $25\%$.

To explain these measurements we give a self-contained analysis of compensation in the layer-wise quadratic model $L(\delta)=\delta^\top H\delta$. Writing the curvature in quantized/free block form, we prove: (i) an exact completion-of-the-square identity whose remainder is the Schur complement $S = A - BD^{-1}B^\top$; (ii) the compensated loss is exactly $u^\top S u$, attained by the unique update $v^\star = -D^{-1}B^\top u$; (iii) compensation never hurts, its gain equals $\|D^{-1}B^\top u\|_D^2$, and the gain is strict if and only if $B^\top u \ne 0$; (iv) the quantized block of $H^{-1}$ is $S^{-1}$, which yields the GPTQ single-column cost $e^2/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$ and the inequality $H_{qq}[H^{-1}]_{qq}\ge 1$; (v) enlarging the compensation window never increases the loss; (vi) the compensated-to-RTN ratio is invariant under rescaling of the error; and (vii) an exact criterion for when compensation lowers a block's share of the total loss. Confronting the theory with the data, we find that the pre-registered bar $\Delta\mathrm{CE}\le 0.15$ is missed in exact arithmetic ($0.1512 - 0.15 = 0.0012$), and that the observed $8.4\%$ drift of the compensation lever between 4 and 3 bits is incompatible with any single quadratic model whose 3-bit error is a rescaling of the 4-bit error.

---

## 1. Introduction

Running a modern language model on commodity hardware — our reference target is a host with 6 GB of memory — requires compressing its weights well below 16 bits. The simplest scheme, round-to-nearest onto a uniform grid, degrades quickly as the bit width drops. Two structural levers are commonly used to improve it:

1. **Grouping**: instead of one grid (scale and zero point) per output channel, use one grid per contiguous group of $g$ input weights (here $g=128$), so that outliers only stretch the grid of their own group.
2. **Compensation**: quantize weights sequentially and, after each rounding decision, update the not-yet-quantized weights to cancel the induced change in the layer output as well as possible. This is the GPTQ algorithm of Frantar, Ashkboos, Hoefler and Alistarh (2022), itself a scalable descendant of the Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) of Hassibi and Stork (1993).

Neither lever is new. The contributions of this paper are:

* **A fixed-protocol ladder.** All arms — per-channel RTN, grouped RTN and grouped GPTQ, at 4 and 3 bits — are measured on one validated harness with a shared reference, protocol and granularity (Section 5).
* **A tail-share quantification.** We measure the contribution of the last two transformer layers to the compensated loss and find it to be $18\%$, smaller than under RTN-style expectations.
* **A complete structural explanation of compensation** in the quadratic model, phrased entirely through the Schur complement, including exact gain formulas, a strictness criterion, window monotonicity, scale invariance, and a tail-share criterion (Sections 2–4).
* **A falsification bridge** between theory and data: the measured drift of the compensation lever certifies that the error shape changes between bit widths (Section 6).

## 2. Setting and definitions

Throughout, all matrices are real. For a symmetric matrix $M$ and vector $x$ write

$$
q_M(x) = x^\top M x .
$$

**Definition 2.1 (Layer-wise quadratic loss).** Let a linear layer with weight row $w\in\mathbb{R}^d$ be evaluated on calibration inputs $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb{R}^d$. The *curvature* is $H = \frac1N\sum_k x_k x_k^\top$ (in practice plus a small damping $\lambda I$). Perturbing the weights by $\delta$ changes the outputs by $\delta^\top x_k$, and the mean squared output change is $L(\delta) = q_H(\delta)$.

**Definition 2.2 (Quantized/free split).** Partition the coordinates into a *quantized* index set $Q$ (of size $m$) and a *free* index set $F$ (of size $n$). Write

$$
H = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B^\top & D\end{pmatrix},\qquad A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m},\; B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\; D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},
$$

and $\delta = (u, v)$, where $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$ is the rounding error on $Q$ (fixed once rounding is done) and $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is the update applied to the free weights (to be chosen). We always assume $D$ is positive definite.

**Definition 2.3 (Schur complement and optimal update).**

$$
S = A - BD^{-1}B^\top, \qquad v^\star(u) = -D^{-1}B^\top u .
$$

**Definition 2.4 (RTN and compensated losses).** The *RTN loss* of an error $u$ is the loss with no update, $L(u,0) = q_A(u)$. The *compensated loss* is $\min_v L(u,v)$. The *compensation lever* is the ratio of the RTN loss to the compensated loss.

**Definition 2.5 ($D$-norm).** For $D$ positive definite, $\|z\|_D^2 = z^\top D z \ge 0$, with equality only for $z = 0$.

## 3. Compensation as a Schur complement

### 3.1 The completion-of-the-square identity

**Theorem 3.1 (OBS split).** For all $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$, $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$,

$$
L(u,v) \;=\; \big\|D^{-1}B^\top u + v\big\|_D^2 \;+\; u^\top S\, u .
$$

*Proof.* Expand $L(u,v) = u^\top A u + 2u^\top B v + v^\top D v$. Expanding the right-hand side, with $z = D^{-1}B^\top u$, gives $z^\top D z + 2 z^\top D v + v^\top D v + u^\top A u - u^\top B D^{-1} B^\top u$. Since $z^\top D z = u^\top BD^{-1}B^\top u$ and $z^\top D v = u^\top B v$ (using symmetry of $D^{-1}$), the two expressions coincide. $\square$

**Lemma 3.2 (RTN sees only the quantized block).** $L(u,0) = q_A(u)$. *Proof.* Immediate from the block expansion. $\square$

### 3.2 Optimality, attainment, uniqueness

**Theorem 3.3 (OBS lower bound).** For every update $v$, $\;u^\top S u \le L(u,v)$.

*Proof.* The first summand in Theorem 3.1 is a $D$-norm, hence non-negative. $\square$

**Theorem 3.4 (Attainment).** $L(u, v^\star(u)) = u^\top S u$.

*Proof.* With $v = v^\star(u)$ the vector inside the $D$-norm is $0$. $\square$

**Theorem 3.5 (Uniqueness).** $L(u,v) = u^\top S u$ if and only if $v = v^\star(u)$.

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.1, equality holds iff $\|D^{-1}B^\top u + v\|_D^2 = 0$, iff $D^{-1}B^\top u + v = 0$ by positive definiteness. $\square$

Hence the compensated loss of Definition 2.4 is exactly $q_S(u)$, and the minimizer is unique.

### 3.3 The exact gain and its strictness

**Theorem 3.6 (Exact compensation gain).**

$$
q_A(u) - q_S(u) \;=\; \big\|D^{-1}B^\top u\big\|_D^2 .
$$

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 3.1 at $v = 0$ and use Lemma 3.2. $\square$

**Corollary 3.7 (Compensation never hurts).** $q_S(u) \le q_A(u)$.

**Theorem 3.8 (Strictness criterion).** $q_S(u) < q_A(u)$ if and only if $B^\top u \ne 0$.

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.6 the gain is positive iff $D^{-1}B^\top u \ne 0$. Since $D$ is invertible, $D^{-1}B^\top u = 0$ iff $B^\top u = 0$. $\square$

Interpretation: compensation strictly helps exactly when the rounding error is correlated, through the cross-curvature $B$, with the weights still free to move. For decorrelated features ($B = 0$) compensation is useless; for strongly correlated features — the norm in transformer activations — it is powerful.

**Proposition 3.9 (Non-negativity).** If the full curvature $H$ is positive semidefinite, then $q_S(u)\ge 0$ for every $u$.

*Proof.* $q_S(u) = L(u,v^\star(u)) = q_H\big((u, v^\star(u))\big) \ge 0$ by Theorem 3.4. $\square$

**Theorem 3.10 (Scale invariance of the lever).** For any $t\ne 0$,

$$
\frac{q_S(tu)}{q_A(tu)} = \frac{q_S(u)}{q_A(u)} .
$$

*Proof.* Quadratic forms are homogeneous of degree two, $q_M(tu) = t^2 q_M(u)$; cancel $t^2 \neq 0$. $\square$

Interpretation: changing the bit width at a fixed error *shape* (a pure rescaling of the error vector, as a coarser grid would induce if all errors scaled together) leaves the compensation lever unchanged.

## 4. The GPTQ column formula and structural consequences

### 4.1 Inverse blocks

**Theorem 4.1 (Block inverse).** If $H$ is invertible and $D$ is positive definite, the $Q\times Q$ block of $H^{-1}$ equals $S^{-1}$.

*Proof sketch.* This is the classical block-inversion formula: when $D$ is invertible and $H$ is invertible, $S$ is invertible and

$$
H^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} S^{-1} & -S^{-1}BD^{-1} \\ -D^{-1}B^\top S^{-1} & D^{-1} + D^{-1}B^\top S^{-1} B D^{-1}\end{pmatrix},
$$

as verified by direct multiplication. $\square$

**Lemma 4.2 (Principal blocks inherit definiteness).** If $H$ is positive definite, so is $D$. *Proof.* For $x\ne 0$, $x^\top D x = (0,x)^\top H (0,x) > 0$. $\square$

### 4.2 The single-column formula

**Theorem 4.3 (GPTQ / OBS column cost).** Let $H$ be positive definite, let $Q = \{q\}$ be a single coordinate quantized with rounding error $e\in\mathbb{R}$, and let all other coordinates be free. Then the optimally compensated loss is

$$
L\big(e, v^\star(e)\big) = \frac{e^2}{[H^{-1}]_{qq}} .
$$

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.4 the loss is $S e^2$ with $S$ a scalar. It is positive: applying Theorem 3.4 with $e = 1$ shows $S = q_H\big((1,v^\star(1))\big) > 0$. By Theorem 4.1, $[H^{-1}]_{qq} = S^{-1}$, so $Se^2 = e^2/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$. $\square$

This is the quantity that drives the GPTQ update: when column $q$ is rounded with error $e_q$, the remaining weights move by $-\frac{e_q}{[H^{-1}]_{qq}}\,[H^{-1}]_{F,q}$, and the loss increases by $e_q^2/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$.

**Corollary 4.4 (Diagonal inequality).** For every positive definite $H$ and every index $q$,

$$
H_{qq}\,[H^{-1}]_{qq} \;\ge\; 1 .
$$

*Proof.* The RTN cost of the error $e = 1$ is $H_{qq}$ (Lemma 3.2), and the compensated cost is $1/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$ (Theorem 4.3). By Corollary 3.7, $1/[H^{-1}]_{qq} \le H_{qq}$; multiply by $[H^{-1}]_{qq} > 0$, which is positive because $H^{-1}$ is positive definite. $\square$

The quantity $1/(H_{qq}[H^{-1}]_{qq})\in(0,1]$ is the fraction of a single column's RTN cost that survives compensation; it equals $1$ exactly when $H_{qF} = 0$ (Theorem 3.8).

### 4.3 Windows

GPTQ implementations restrict updates to a "lazy" block of columns aligned with the quantization groups. The following shows this restriction can only cost, never gain.

**Theorem 4.5 (Wider windows never hurt).** Split the free set as $F = F_1 \sqcup F_2$ and let $S_1$ be the Schur complement computed using only $F_1$ as free set (i.e. with $B$ and $D$ replaced by their $F_1$-columns and $F_1\times F_1$ block). Then for every $u$,

$$
q_S(u) \;\le\; q_{S_1}(u).
$$

*Proof.* The $F_1\times F_1$ block of $D$ is positive definite (Lemma 4.2 applied to $D$). Freezing the $F_2$ weights at zero turns the full problem into the restricted one: $L\big(u,(v_1,0)\big)$ equals the restricted loss of $(u,v_1)$. Taking $v_1$ to be the restricted optimum, the restricted optimal value $q_{S_1}(u)$ is one particular value of the full loss, which by Theorem 3.3 is at least $q_S(u)$. $\square$

### 4.4 Tail share

**Theorem 4.6 (Tail-share criterion).** Let a *core* and a *tail* block have RTN costs $a,b>0$ and compensation gains $g_a<a$, $g_b<b$. Then compensation strictly lowers the tail's share of the total loss,

$$
\frac{b-g_b}{(a-g_a)+(b-g_b)} \;<\; \frac{b}{a+b},
$$

if and only if

$$
\frac{g_a}{a} < \frac{g_b}{b}.
$$

*Proof.* All denominators are positive. Cross-multiplying, the first inequality is $(b-g_b)(a+b) < b\,(a+b-g_a-g_b)$, which simplifies to $b\,g_a < a\,g_b$; dividing by $ab>0$ gives the second. $\square$

Combined with Theorem 3.6, the per-block gains are $g = \|D^{-1}B^\top u\|_D^2$ for the respective blocks, so the tail share falls precisely when the tail's errors are proportionally better correlated with their free weights.

## 5. The experiment

### 5.1 Protocol

* **Model:** Qwen2.5-0.5B (24 transformer layers), evaluation context 512 tokens.
* **Metric:** $\Delta\mathrm{CE}$, the increase of next-token cross-entropy over the unquantized model, and *retained accuracy*, the ratio of quantized to unquantized next-token accuracy. The unquantized baseline (accuracy $0.4460$, cross-entropy $2.8697$) was reproduced exactly before any arm was run.
* **GPTQ implementation:** sequential layer-wise processing, with inputs to each layer recaptured from the already-quantized prefix of the network; curvature accumulated by hooks on the actual linear modules; quantization blocks aligned to groups of 128; Cholesky factorization of the damped inverse curvature, retried with escalating damping on failure (schedule fixed before the run). Calibration: 16 sequences drawn from the training side only. No column reordering ("act-order").
* **Reference floors** (from the preceding round, same harness): per-channel 4-bit RTN $+0.788$; grouped 4-bit RTN $+0.318$; per-channel 6-bit RTN $+0.035$; per-channel 3-bit RTN $+9.23$; grouped 3-bit RTN $+2.72$.

### 5.2 Results

| Arm | $\Delta\mathrm{CE}$ | retained accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| GPTQ 4-bit $g{=}128$, all layers | $+0.1512$ | $0.9546$ |
| GPTQ 4-bit $g{=}128$, core (layers 0–21) | $+0.1235$ | $0.9641$ |
| GPTQ 3-bit $g{=}128$, all layers | $+1.1932$ | $0.7086$ |

The full ladder:

| bits | per-channel RTN | grouped RTN | grouped GPTQ | grouping lever | compensation lever | compounded |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | $0.788$ | $0.318$ | $0.1512$ | $2.478$ | $2.103$ | $5.212$ |
| 3 | $9.23$ | $2.72$ | $1.1932$ | $3.393$ | $2.280$ | $7.736$ |

### 5.3 Pre-registered predictions, assessed in exact arithmetic

* **P1** ($\Delta\mathrm{CE}\le 0.15$ for GPTQ 4-bit): **missed.** $0.1512 - 0.15 = 0.0012 > 0$. (The run's own log described this as confirmed "at the boundary"; the exact comparison does not support that reading. The substantive finding — a $2.10\times$ improvement over grouped RTN — stands.)
* **P2** ($\Delta\mathrm{CE}\le 0.14$, approaching the 6-bit per-channel floor): **refuted.**
* **P3** (the final two layers contribute more than $25\%$ of the compensated loss): **refuted.** The tail increment is exactly $0.1512 - 0.1235 = 0.0277$, and the share $0.0277/0.1512 \approx 0.1832$ lies strictly between $1/6$ and $1/5$.

### 5.4 Deployment table (6 GB host)

| scheme | usable at | cost |
|---|---|---|
| per-channel RTN | $\ge 6$ bits | $+0.035$ at 6 bits; $+0.788$ at 4 bits |
| grouped RTN | 4 bits | $+0.32$ |
| grouped GPTQ | 4 bits (3 bits survivable) | $+0.15$ (3 bits: $+1.19$) |

### 5.5 Engineering hazards

Three silent errors were caught before the reported runs: (1) hooks registered on container modules rather than linear modules, detected by checking the width of captured activations; (2) a broadcasting error in per-column scales; (3) loss of numerical positive definiteness of the curvature computed from partially quantized activations, handled by escalating damping. A single-matrix regression test is retained: on one random layer, GPTQ must beat RTN on layer-output error. Corollary 3.7 guarantees that each compensation step cannot hurt *for the error it corrects*; since compensation also changes the weights rounded later, and hence their rounding errors, the end-to-end comparison is an empirical check rather than a theorem.

## 6. Theory meets data

**Proposition 6.1 (Exact ladder facts).** In exact rational arithmetic:

1. $0.1512 > 0.15$, with difference $0.0012$.
2. The tail increment is $0.0277$ and $1/6 < 0.0277/0.1512 < 1/5$.
3. The 4-bit compensation lever satisfies $2.1 \le 0.318/0.1512 < 2.11$.
4. The compensation lever drifts by less than $9\%$: $1 < \dfrac{2.72/1.1932}{0.318/0.1512} < 1.09$.
5. The grouping lever drifts by more than $35\%$: $\dfrac{9.23/2.72}{0.788/0.318} > 1.35$.
6. The compounded lever exceeds $5$ at 4 bits and $7.7$ at 3 bits.

*Proof.* Direct computation with the rational values. $\square$

**Theorem 6.2 (No single rescaled quadratic model).** There are no matrices $A,B,D$ (with $D$ invertible), error vector $u$, and scalar $t\ne0$ such that simultaneously

$$
q_A(u) = 0.318,\quad q_S(u) = 0.1512,\quad q_A(tu) = 2.72,\quad q_S(tu) = 1.1932 .
$$

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.10 the ratios $q_S/q_A$ at $u$ and at $tu$ coincide, but $0.1512/0.318 \neq 1.1932/2.72$ (cross-multiplying: $0.1512\cdot 2.72 = 0.411264 \ne 0.379437\ldots = 1.1932\cdot 0.318$). $\square$

*Interpretation.* Within the quadratic model, the $8.4\%$ drift of the compensation lever cannot be a scale effect. It must reflect a change of error **shape** between bit widths — the pattern of rounding directions, and in particular clipping at group extremes — or a departure of the true loss from its quadratic approximation. The much larger drift of the grouping lever is consistent with grouping being intrinsically a shape-changing operation: it removes outlier-driven grid stretching, whose damage grows as the grid coarsens.

**Reading the tail share.** By Theorem 4.6, the observed $18\%$ compensated tail share is smaller than the RTN tail share if and only if compensation's relative gain in layers 22–23 exceeds that in layers 0–21. The RTN core-only arm, a single cheap run, would decide this.

## 7. Algorithms

**Algorithm 1 (Column-sequential GPTQ for one weight row).** Input: weights $w\in\mathbb{R}^d$, damped curvature $H_\lambda = H+\lambda I$, bit width $b$, group size $g$.

1. Compute $H_\lambda^{-1}$ and its upper Cholesky factor $U$ ($H_\lambda^{-1} = U^\top U$). On failure, increase $\lambda$ and retry.
2. For $q = 1,\dots,d$:
   1. If $q$ starts a group, fix the group's grid (scale and zero point) from the *current* weights $w_{q:q+g-1}$.
   2. $\hat w_q \leftarrow \mathrm{round}(w_q)$ on the group grid; $\varepsilon \leftarrow (w_q - \hat w_q)/U_{qq}$.
   3. $w_j \leftarrow w_j - \varepsilon\, U_{qj}$ for all $j>q$.
3. Return $\hat w$.

$U_{qq}^2$ equals the $(q,q)$ entry of the inverse of the trailing block $H_\lambda[q{:},q{:}]$, so step 2.2–2.3 is precisely the OBS update of Theorem 4.3 applied to the current free set $\{q+1,\dots,d\}$; summing these per-column costs reproduces the final loss (numerically exact in our demonstrations). The cost is $O(d^3)$ for the factorization plus $O(d^2)$ per row; the factorization is shared across all rows of a layer.

**Algorithm 2 (Fixed-protocol ladder).** For each bit width $b\in\{4,3\}$ and each arm (per-channel RTN, grouped RTN, grouped GPTQ), quantize all target linear modules with the same reference model, calibration data, evaluation set and grouping, and report $\Delta\mathrm{CE}$ and retained accuracy; compute grouping, compensation and compounded levers as ratios of successive floors.

## 8. Discussion

**What the theory says.** Compensation is exactly the elimination of the free weights from a quadratic form. Its floor is the Schur complement, reached by a unique linear correction; its gain is a $D$-energy that vanishes iff the error is uncorrelated with the free weights. The ubiquity of the Schur complement explains the success of GPTQ without appeal to any specific property of language models beyond correlated activations.

**What the data say.** On a real 0.5B model, the compensation lever is about $2.1$–$2.3\times$, compounding with grouping to more than $5\times$ (4 bits) and $7.7\times$ (3 bits). The last two layers remain measurably more expensive, but compensation compresses their share.

**Limitations.** The guarantees of Sections 3–4 concern a fixed error vector; in sequential quantization the later rounding errors depend on earlier updates, so the end-to-end superiority of GPTQ over RTN is empirical (it held in every measured arm). One model; context 512; no act-order; 16 calibration sequences; the quadratic model is a local surrogate for cross-entropy, so theorems about $q_H$ constrain the data only through that surrogate. Theorem 6.2 is a statement about the quadratic model: it shows the measured pairs cannot be explained by error rescaling within it, not that cross-entropy is or is not quadratic.

## 9. Future work

1. **Correlation-spectrum law.** Conjecture: under independent uniform rounding errors, the expected GPTQ/RTN ratio for a layer is $\operatorname{tr}\big(\operatorname{diag}(H^{-1})^{-1}\big)/\operatorname{tr}(H)$ up to sequential-order corrections, so the lever is predictable from the curvature alone (Theorem 4.3 gives the per-column compensated cost $\mathbb{E}[e^2]/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$ against the RTN cost $\mathbb{E}[e^2]H_{qq}$).
2. **Sequential telescoping and act-order.** Conjecture: the total loss of column-sequential GPTQ equals $\sum_q e_q^2/d_q$ with $d_q$ the successive pivots (via the Crabtree–Haynsworth quotient property of iterated Schur complements), and processing columns by descending $H_{qq}$ minimizes the worst-case bound $\sum_q (s_q^2/4)/d_q$, with $s_q$ the grid step.
3. **Tail-share compression.** If tail errors are relatively better correlated with free weights, the RTN tail share at 4 bits should exceed $18\%$; one RTN core-only run tests this via Theorem 4.6.
4. **Shape-drift decomposition.** The 4→3-bit lever drift $2.103\to2.280$ should be explained by the change of normalized error direction $u/\|u\|$ and may vanish after re-scaling 3-bit errors by grouped clipping statistics.
5. **Engineering:** act-order variant, a joint weight + KV-cache budget optimizer, tail-aware mixed precision keeping layers 22–23 at higher bit width, and transfer to Qwen2.5-1.5B.

## 10. Conclusion

A century-old identity — completing the square in block form — fully accounts for the mechanics of compensated quantization: the unavoidable cost is a Schur complement, the avoidable cost is removed by a unique update, and the gain is strict exactly when errors and free weights are correlated. On a real 0.5B model, this mechanism halves the damage of grouped rounding at 4 bits and makes 3-bit weights survivable, while the residual drift of its lever tells us that coarser grids change the *shape* of the rounding error, not merely its size.

## A model that will not fit

Imagine you want to run a language model on a modest machine — a laptop with 6 GB of memory, say. The model's knowledge lives in its weights: hundreds of millions of real numbers, each normally stored with 16 bits of precision. To make it fit, you want to store each weight with only 4 bits, or even 3. Four bits give you exactly $2^4 = 16$ possible values per weight; three bits give you only $8$.

The obvious way to do this is called **round-to-nearest** (RTN). Lay down a ruler with 16 evenly spaced tick marks covering the range of the weights, and move every weight to its nearest tick. It is simple, fast, and — as anyone who has tried it knows — it can be surprisingly destructive.

In a recent series of experiments on a half-billion-parameter language model (Qwen2.5-0.5B), the damage was measured by the increase in *cross-entropy*, written $\Delta\mathrm{CE}$: how much more "surprised" the compressed model is by real text than the original. A $\Delta\mathrm{CE}$ of $0$ means no harm at all; a few tenths is tolerable; anything above $1$ means the model has lost much of its competence.

The results tell a story in three acts:

| Method | 4 bits | 3 bits |
|---|---|---|
| One ruler per output channel (per-channel RTN) | $+0.788$ | $+9.23$ |
| One ruler per group of 128 weights (grouped RTN) | $+0.318$ | $+2.72$ |
| Grouped rounding **with compensation** (GPTQ) | $+0.151$ | $+1.19$ |

At 3 bits, naive rounding wrecks the model ($+9.23$ — essentially gibberish). Using finer rulers helps a lot. But the final row, which adds an idea called **compensation**, roughly halves the damage again, bringing the 3-bit model back from the dead.

This article is about that last row: what compensation is, why it must work, exactly how much it can help, and what the numbers secretly reveal.

## The idea: if you must make an error, make the others fix it

Suppose you are packing a suitcase to an exact weight limit, and each item has to be swapped for a slightly heavier or lighter standard-size version. If you swap the first item and it comes out $200$ grams too heavy, you would not just carry on swapping the rest independently. You would choose the remaining items to *absorb* that $200$ grams.

Compensation does the same with weights. Process the weights one at a time (or one block at a time). Round the current weight — committing an error you can no longer undo — and then nudge all the *not-yet-rounded* weights so that the layer's output changes as little as possible. Then round the next one, nudge the rest again, and so on.

This is the core of an algorithm called **GPTQ**, published by Frantar and collaborators in 2022, which in turn descends from the "Optimal Brain Surgeon" of Hassibi and Stork from 1993. The algorithm itself is prior art. What is new here is a clean mathematical account of *why* it helps, *exactly how much*, and what that says about the measurements above.

## What "as little as possible" means

A neural network layer takes an input vector $x$ and produces $w \cdot x$ for each row of weights $w$. If we perturb the weights by a small error $\delta$, the output changes by $\delta \cdot x$. Averaging the squared change over a batch of real "calibration" inputs gives

$$
L(\delta) = \delta^{\top} H\, \delta, \qquad H = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k} x_k x_k^{\top}.
$$

The matrix $H$ is the **curvature**: it tells us which directions of error matter. If two input features tend to fire together, their entries in $H$ are strongly linked, and an error in one weight can be cancelled by an opposite error in the other. That linkage is precisely what compensation exploits.

Now split the weights into two camps: the ones we are rounding right now (error $u$, fixed — we cannot change it), and the ones still free (adjustment $v$, ours to choose). The curvature splits into blocks:

$$
H = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B^{\top} & D \end{pmatrix}.
$$

Here $A$ describes how the rounded weights interact with each other, $D$ how the free weights interact with each other, and $B$ — the crucial piece — how the two camps are coupled.

## The square that completes itself

The central fact is an identity every algebra student meets in a simple form: **completing the square.** Just as $a x^2 + 2bx + c$ can be rewritten as $a(x + b/a)^2 + (c - b^2/a)$, the loss can be rewritten exactly as

$$
L(u, v) \;=\; \underbrace{\big\| D^{-1}B^{\top}u + v \big\|_D^2}_{\text{depends on our choice } v}
\;+\; \underbrace{u^{\top}\big(A - B D^{-1}B^{\top}\big)u}_{\text{the unavoidable part}},
$$

where $\|z\|_D^2 = z^{\top} D z$ is a weighted length, always non-negative.

The matrix $S = A - BD^{-1}B^{\top}$ in the second term is famous: it is the **Schur complement**, named after Issai Schur, who used it in 1917, although the determinant identity behind it is older still. It is the curvature of the rounded weights *after* the free weights have done everything they can.

Everything follows from this one rewriting.

**The best you can do.** The first term is never negative, so no adjustment can push the loss below $u^{\top} S u$. *Compensation has a hard floor, and that floor is the Schur complement.*

**How to get there.** Choose $v^\star = -D^{-1}B^{\top}u$. This makes the first term exactly zero, and the floor is attained.

**There is only one way.** Because $D$ is positive definite, the first term is zero *only* when $v = v^\star$. The optimal correction is unique — there is no other set of nudges that does as well.

**Compensation never hurts.** Plain rounding corresponds to $v = 0$, whose loss is $u^{\top}Au$. Since the floor is the minimum over all $v$, it is at most this. More precisely, the gain is exactly

$$
u^{\top}Au \;-\; u^{\top}Su \;=\; \big\|D^{-1}B^{\top}u\big\|_D^2 .
$$

**When it helps strictly.** That gain is positive *if and only if* $B^{\top}u \neq 0$ — that is, exactly when the rounding error is correlated, through the curvature, with the weights still free to move. If the rounded and free weights never interact, there is nothing to compensate with. In real networks, input features are heavily correlated, so the coupling $B$ is large and the gain is real.

## One weight at a time: the GPTQ formula

Specialise to rounding a single weight $q$ with error $e$. The Schur complement is then just a number, and a classical fact about block matrices says the top-left entry of $H^{-1}$ is exactly $1/S$. So the cost of rounding weight $q$ with perfect compensation is

$$
\text{compensated cost} = \frac{e^2}{[H^{-1}]_{qq}}, \qquad \text{while plain rounding costs} \quad H_{qq}\, e^2 .
$$

This is exactly the quantity that the GPTQ algorithm uses at each step. Since compensation never hurts, comparing the two costs yields a neat inequality, valid for every positive definite matrix:

$$
H_{qq}\,\big[H^{-1}\big]_{qq} \;\ge\; 1 .
$$

The ratio $1/(H_{qq}[H^{-1}]_{qq})$ is precisely the fraction of a single weight's rounding cost that survives compensation. When features are independent, $H$ is diagonal, the product equals $1$, and compensation does nothing. The more correlated the features, the larger the product, and the more the error can be absorbed.

## Two more guarantees

**Wider windows never hurt.** Real implementations do not let every remaining weight participate in every correction; they work in blocks of columns aligned with the groups of 128 that share a ruler. Is a restricted window a loss? Only in one direction: allowing more free weights to participate can never increase the floor. Freezing some free weights at zero is just one particular (generally suboptimal) choice in the larger problem.

**The lever does not care about scale.** Going from 4 to 3 bits roughly doubles the spacing of the ruler. If that simply multiplied every rounding error by the same factor $t$, both the compensated and the uncompensated losses would be multiplied by $t^2$, and their *ratio* would not budge. The compensation lever — how many times better GPTQ is than plain rounding — is invariant under rescaling the error.

## What the numbers say

With the theory in hand, the measurements become a laboratory notebook to check against.

**The headline lever.** At 4 bits, grouped rounding gives $0.318$ and GPTQ gives $0.1512$: a ratio of about $2.10$. Compensation cancels a little over half of the damage.

**A pre-registered bar, honestly assessed.** Before the run, the experiment set a target: GPTQ at 4 bits should reach $\Delta\mathrm{CE} \le 0.15$. The measurement, $0.1512$, was originally reported as meeting the bar "at the boundary." In exact arithmetic it does not: $0.1512$ exceeds $0.15$ by $0.0012$. It is a near miss, and the honest verdict is that the bar was missed. A second, stricter target of $0.14$ was missed clearly.

**The tail is real but small.** Earlier work had suggested the final two of the model's 24 transformer layers carry a disproportionate share of the quantization damage. Quantizing only layers 0–21 with GPTQ gives $0.1235$; quantizing all layers gives $0.1512$. The last two layers therefore add $0.0277$ — about $18\%$ of the total, strictly between one sixth and one fifth, and well short of the predicted "more than a quarter." Compensation seems to have shrunk the tail's outsized cost.

There is a crisp algebraic criterion for when this can happen. Suppose the core and tail have plain-rounding costs $a$ and $b$, and compensation removes amounts $g_a$ and $g_b$. Then the tail's share of the total *drops* if and only if

$$
\frac{g_a}{a} < \frac{g_b}{b},
$$

that is, if and only if compensation helps the tail *proportionally more* than the core. The measured 18% is therefore evidence — testable by a single additional run of plain rounding on the core — that the final layers' errors are especially well correlated with their free weights.

**The ladder of levers.** Look at the table as a ladder:

- At 4 bits: $0.788 \to 0.318 \to 0.151$ (grouping gives about $2.5\times$, compensation about $2.1\times$).
- At 3 bits: $9.23 \to 2.72 \to 1.19$ (grouping about $3.4\times$, compensation about $2.3\times$).

Each structural lever multiplies the previous floor down. The combined lever is more than $5\times$ at 4 bits and more than $7.7\times$ at 3 bits.

## A detective's clue: the lever drifts

Here is where the scale-invariance theorem earns its keep. If going from 4 to 3 bits merely scaled every error by the same factor, the compensation lever would be identical at both bit widths. It is not: $2.10$ at 4 bits, $2.28$ at 3 bits — a drift of about $8\%$.

That small number carries a definite logical consequence: **there is no single quadratic model, with any curvature whatsoever, in which the 3-bit error vector is merely a rescaled copy of the 4-bit one and which reproduces both measured pairs.** The drift must come from a change in the *shape* of the error — which weights get rounded up versus down, how clipping at the extremes of each group behaves — or from the true loss bending away from its quadratic approximation.

The grouping lever drifts much more, by more than $35\%$ (from about $2.5$ to $3.4$). That too makes sense: grouping is fundamentally a shape-changing operation. By giving each block of 128 weights its own ruler, it stops a single outlier from stretching the ruler for everyone, so its benefit grows as the ruler gets coarser. Compensation, by contrast, is a linear correction applied after rounding, and its lever is nearly — but measurably not quite — scale-free.

## What it means on a real machine

For a 6 GB machine, the practical conclusions are blunt:

- Per-channel rounding is unusable below 6 bits (at 6 bits it costs only $+0.035$, but at 4 bits it costs $+0.788$).
- Grouped rounding is viable at 4 bits ($+0.32$).
- Grouped GPTQ is comfortable at 4 bits ($+0.15$) and *survivable* at 3 bits ($+1.19$) — a regime where naive rounding produces nonsense.

The experiment was deliberately honest about its limits: one model, a 512-token context, 16 calibration sequences, and no column reordering ("act-order"). The calibration data came only from the training side, and the baseline numbers were reproduced exactly before any comparison.

Getting there involved catching three silent bugs that would have quietly corrupted the science: hooks attached to container modules rather than the actual linear layers, a broadcasting error in per-column scales, and a Cholesky factorization that failed because partially quantized activations made the curvature numerically indefinite (fixed by a damping term that escalates on failure). A tiny regression test now guards the implementation: on a single matrix, GPTQ must beat plain rounding on the layer-output error. The theorem that compensation never hurts guarantees that each individual correction step cannot make things worse for the error it is correcting; because those corrections also shift the weights that are rounded later, the end-to-end win is something to check, and the test checks it.

## What comes next

The Schur-complement picture suggests sharp, testable questions.

- **Can the lever be predicted from the curvature alone?** Averaged over random rounding errors, per-column compensation costs scale like $1/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$ while plain rounding costs scale like $H_{qq}$, so the ratio $\sum_q 1/[H^{-1}]_{qq} \big/ \sum_q H_{qq}$ is a natural candidate predictor — up to corrections from the order in which columns are processed.
- **Does order matter, and which order is best?** Iterated Schur complements obey a "quotient" rule that should make the total cost of sequential compensation telescope into a sum of per-column pivot costs. Processing columns with the largest curvature first ("act-order") is the natural candidate optimum.
- **Mixed precision for the tail.** Keeping the last two layers at higher precision is cheap and directly targets that 18%.
- **Scale.** Does the $2\times$ lever survive on a model three times larger?

## The moral

Rounding is irreversible: once a weight is snapped to a grid point, that information is gone. But the *consequences* of an error are not fixed — they depend on what you do next. The completion-of-the-square identity makes this precise. Every rounding error has an unavoidable part, the Schur complement, and an avoidable part, which a unique correction of the remaining weights removes entirely. The more the weights talk to each other, the bigger the avoidable part, and the more there is to gain.

A century-old piece of matrix algebra, in other words, is the reason a 3-bit language model can still speak.

## Abstract

We study post-training weight quantization of a pretrained language model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) on a single fixed evaluation protocol, comparing per-channel round-to-nearest (RTN), grouped RTN (group size 128), and sequential, curvature-compensated quantization (GPTQ, group size 128) at matched bit widths. At 4 bits, GPTQ attains a cross-entropy increase of $\Delta\mathrm{CE} = +0.1512$ (retained next-token accuracy $0.9546$), a factor $2.10$ better than grouped RTN ($+0.318$) and $5.21$ better than per-channel RTN ($+0.788$). At 3 bits, GPTQ rescues the model from $+9.23$ (per-channel RTN) and $+2.72$ (grouped RTN) to $+1.19$. The final two transformer layers contribute $0.0277$, i.e. $18.3\%$ of the compensated loss, refuting a pre-registered prediction of more than $25\%$.

To explain these measurements we give a self-contained analysis of compensation in the layer-wise quadratic model $L(\delta)=\delta^\top H\delta$. Writing the curvature in quantized/free block form, we prove: (i) an exact completion-of-the-square identity whose remainder is the Schur complement $S = A - BD^{-1}B^\top$; (ii) the compensated loss is exactly $u^\top S u$, attained by the unique update $v^\star = -D^{-1}B^\top u$; (iii) compensation never hurts, its gain equals $\|D^{-1}B^\top u\|_D^2$, and the gain is strict if and only if $B^\top u \ne 0$; (iv) the quantized block of $H^{-1}$ is $S^{-1}$, which yields the GPTQ single-column cost $e^2/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$ and the inequality $H_{qq}[H^{-1}]_{qq}\ge 1$; (v) enlarging the compensation window never increases the loss; (vi) the compensated-to-RTN ratio is invariant under rescaling of the error; and (vii) an exact criterion for when compensation lowers a block's share of the total loss. Confronting the theory with the data, we find that the pre-registered bar $\Delta\mathrm{CE}\le 0.15$ is missed in exact arithmetic ($0.1512 - 0.15 = 0.0012$), and that the observed $8.4\%$ drift of the compensation lever between 4 and 3 bits is incompatible with any single quadratic model whose 3-bit error is a rescaling of the 4-bit error.

## 1. Introduction

Running a modern language model on commodity hardware — our reference target is a host with 6 GB of memory — requires compressing its weights well below 16 bits. The simplest scheme, round-to-nearest onto a uniform grid, degrades quickly as the bit width drops. Two structural levers are commonly used to improve it:

1. **Grouping**: instead of one grid (scale and zero point) per output channel, use one grid per contiguous group of $g$ input weights (here $g=128$), so that outliers only stretch the grid of their own group.
2. **Compensation**: quantize weights sequentially and, after each rounding decision, update the not-yet-quantized weights to cancel the induced change in the layer output as well as possible. This is the GPTQ algorithm of Frantar, Ashkboos, Hoefler and Alistarh (2022), itself a scalable descendant of the Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) of Hassibi and Stork (1993).

Neither lever is new. The contributions of this paper are:

* **A fixed-protocol ladder.** All arms — per-channel RTN, grouped RTN and grouped GPTQ, at 4 and 3 bits — are measured on one validated harness with a shared reference, protocol and granularity (Section 5).
* **A tail-share quantification.** We measure the contribution of the last two transformer layers to the compensated loss and find it to be $18\%$, smaller than under RTN-style expectations.
* **A complete structural explanation of compensation** in the quadratic model, phrased entirely through the Schur complement, including exact gain formulas, a strictness criterion, window monotonicity, scale invariance, and a tail-share criterion (Sections 2–4).
* **A falsification bridge** between theory and data: the measured drift of the compensation lever certifies that the error shape changes between bit widths (Section 6).

## 2. Setting and definitions

Throughout, all matrices are real. For a symmetric matrix $M$ and vector $x$ write

$$
q_M(x) = x^\top M x .
$$

**Definition 2.1 (Layer-wise quadratic loss).** Let a linear layer with weight row $w\in\mathbb{R}^d$ be evaluated on calibration inputs $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\mathbb{R}^d$. The *curvature* is $H = \frac1N\sum_k x_k x_k^\top$ (in practice plus a small damping $\lambda I$). Perturbing the weights by $\delta$ changes the outputs by $\delta^\top x_k$, and the mean squared output change is $L(\delta) = q_H(\delta)$.

**Definition 2.2 (Quantized/free split).** Partition the coordinates into a *quantized* index set $Q$ (of size $m$) and a *free* index set $F$ (of size $n$). Write

$$
H = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B^\top & D\end{pmatrix},\qquad A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m},\; B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\; D\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},
$$

and $\delta = (u, v)$, where $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$ is the rounding error on $Q$ (fixed once rounding is done) and $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is the update applied to the free weights (to be chosen). We always assume $D$ is positive definite.

**Definition 2.3 (Schur complement and optimal update).**

$$
S = A - BD^{-1}B^\top, \qquad v^\star(u) = -D^{-1}B^\top u .
$$

**Definition 2.4 (RTN and compensated losses).** The *RTN loss* of an error $u$ is the loss with no update, $L(u,0) = q_A(u)$. The *compensated loss* is $\min_v L(u,v)$. The *compensation lever* is the ratio of the RTN loss to the compensated loss.

**Definition 2.5 ($D$-norm).** For $D$ positive definite, $\|z\|_D^2 = z^\top D z \ge 0$, with equality only for $z = 0$.

## 3. Compensation as a Schur complement

### 3.1 The completion-of-the-square identity

**Theorem 3.1 (OBS split).** For all $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$, $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$,

$$
L(u,v) \;=\; \big\|D^{-1}B^\top u + v\big\|_D^2 \;+\; u^\top S\, u .
$$

*Proof.* Expand $L(u,v) = u^\top A u + 2u^\top B v + v^\top D v$. Expanding the right-hand side, with $z = D^{-1}B^\top u$, gives $z^\top D z + 2 z^\top D v + v^\top D v + u^\top A u - u^\top B D^{-1} B^\top u$. Since $z^\top D z = u^\top BD^{-1}B^\top u$ and $z^\top D v = u^\top B v$ (using symmetry of $D^{-1}$), the two expressions coincide. $\square$

**Lemma 3.2 (RTN sees only the quantized block).** $L(u,0) = q_A(u)$. *Proof.* Immediate from the block expansion. $\square$

### 3.2 Optimality, attainment, uniqueness

**Theorem 3.3 (OBS lower bound).** For every update $v$, $\;u^\top S u \le L(u,v)$.

*Proof.* The first summand in Theorem 3.1 is a $D$-norm, hence non-negative. $\square$

**Theorem 3.4 (Attainment).** $L(u, v^\star(u)) = u^\top S u$.

*Proof.* With $v = v^\star(u)$ the vector inside the $D$-norm is $0$. $\square$

**Theorem 3.5 (Uniqueness).** $L(u,v) = u^\top S u$ if and only if $v = v^\star(u)$.

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.1, equality holds iff $\|D^{-1}B^\top u + v\|_D^2 = 0$, iff $D^{-1}B^\top u + v = 0$ by positive definiteness. $\square$

Hence the compensated loss of Definition 2.4 is exactly $q_S(u)$, and the minimizer is unique.

### 3.3 The exact gain and its strictness

**Theorem 3.6 (Exact compensation gain).**

$$
q_A(u) - q_S(u) \;=\; \big\|D^{-1}B^\top u\big\|_D^2 .
$$

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 3.1 at $v = 0$ and use Lemma 3.2. $\square$

**Corollary 3.7 (Compensation never hurts).** $q_S(u) \le q_A(u)$.

**Theorem 3.8 (Strictness criterion).** $q_S(u) < q_A(u)$ if and only if $B^\top u \ne 0$.

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.6 the gain is positive iff $D^{-1}B^\top u \ne 0$. Since $D$ is invertible, $D^{-1}B^\top u = 0$ iff $B^\top u = 0$. $\square$

Interpretation: compensation strictly helps exactly when the rounding error is correlated, through the cross-curvature $B$, with the weights still free to move. For decorrelated features ($B = 0$) compensation is useless; for strongly correlated features — the norm in transformer activations — it is powerful.

**Proposition 3.9 (Non-negativity).** If the full curvature $H$ is positive semidefinite, then $q_S(u)\ge 0$ for every $u$.

*Proof.* $q_S(u) = L(u,v^\star(u)) = q_H\big((u, v^\star(u))\big) \ge 0$ by Theorem 3.4. $\square$

**Theorem 3.10 (Scale invariance of the lever).** For any $t\ne 0$,

$$
\frac{q_S(tu)}{q_A(tu)} = \frac{q_S(u)}{q_A(u)} .
$$

*Proof.* Quadratic forms are homogeneous of degree two, $q_M(tu) = t^2 q_M(u)$; cancel $t^2 \neq 0$. $\square$

Interpretation: changing the bit width at a fixed error *shape* (a pure rescaling of the error vector, as a coarser grid would induce if all errors scaled together) leaves the compensation lever unchanged.

## 4. The GPTQ column formula and structural consequences

### 4.1 Inverse blocks

**Theorem 4.1 (Block inverse).** If $H$ is invertible and $D$ is positive definite, the $Q\times Q$ block of $H^{-1}$ equals $S^{-1}$.

*Proof sketch.* This is the classical block-inversion formula: when $D$ is invertible and $H$ is invertible, $S$ is invertible and

$$
H^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} S^{-1} & -S^{-1}BD^{-1} \\ -D^{-1}B^\top S^{-1} & D^{-1} + D^{-1}B^\top S^{-1} B D^{-1}\end{pmatrix},
$$

as verified by direct multiplication. $\square$

**Lemma 4.2 (Principal blocks inherit definiteness).** If $H$ is positive definite, so is $D$. *Proof.* For $x\ne 0$, $x^\top D x = (0,x)^\top H (0,x) > 0$. $\square$

### 4.2 The single-column formula

**Theorem 4.3 (GPTQ / OBS column cost).** Let $H$ be positive definite, let $Q = \{q\}$ be a single coordinate quantized with rounding error $e\in\mathbb{R}$, and let all other coordinates be free. Then the optimally compensated loss is

$$
L\big(e, v^\star(e)\big) = \frac{e^2}{[H^{-1}]_{qq}} .
$$

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.4 the loss is $S e^2$ with $S$ a scalar. It is positive: applying Theorem 3.4 with $e = 1$ shows $S = q_H\big((1,v^\star(1))\big) > 0$. By Theorem 4.1, $[H^{-1}]_{qq} = S^{-1}$, so $Se^2 = e^2/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$. $\square$

This is the quantity that drives the GPTQ update: when column $q$ is rounded with error $e_q$, the remaining weights move by $-\frac{e_q}{[H^{-1}]_{qq}}\,[H^{-1}]_{F,q}$, and the loss increases by $e_q^2/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$.

**Corollary 4.4 (Diagonal inequality).** For every positive definite $H$ and every index $q$,

$$
H_{qq}\,[H^{-1}]_{qq} \;\ge\; 1 .
$$

*Proof.* The RTN cost of the error $e = 1$ is $H_{qq}$ (Lemma 3.2), and the compensated cost is $1/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$ (Theorem 4.3). By Corollary 3.7, $1/[H^{-1}]_{qq} \le H_{qq}$; multiply by $[H^{-1}]_{qq} > 0$, which is positive because $H^{-1}$ is positive definite. $\square$

The quantity $1/(H_{qq}[H^{-1}]_{qq})\in(0,1]$ is the fraction of a single column's RTN cost that survives compensation; it equals $1$ exactly when $H_{qF} = 0$ (Theorem 3.8).

### 4.3 Windows

GPTQ implementations restrict updates to a "lazy" block of columns aligned with the quantization groups. The following shows this restriction can only cost, never gain.

**Theorem 4.5 (Wider windows never hurt).** Split the free set as $F = F_1 \sqcup F_2$ and let $S_1$ be the Schur complement computed using only $F_1$ as free set (i.e. with $B$ and $D$ replaced by their $F_1$-columns and $F_1\times F_1$ block). Then for every $u$,

$$
q_S(u) \;\le\; q_{S_1}(u).
$$

*Proof.* The $F_1\times F_1$ block of $D$ is positive definite (Lemma 4.2 applied to $D$). Freezing the $F_2$ weights at zero turns the full problem into the restricted one: $L\big(u,(v_1,0)\big)$ equals the restricted loss of $(u,v_1)$. Taking $v_1$ to be the restricted optimum, the restricted optimal value $q_{S_1}(u)$ is one particular value of the full loss, which by Theorem 3.3 is at least $q_S(u)$. $\square$

### 4.4 Tail share

**Theorem 4.6 (Tail-share criterion).** Let a *core* and a *tail* block have RTN costs $a,b>0$ and compensation gains $g_a<a$, $g_b<b$. Then compensation strictly lowers the tail's share of the total loss,

$$
\frac{b-g_b}{(a-g_a)+(b-g_b)} \;<\; \frac{b}{a+b},
$$

if and only if

$$
\frac{g_a}{a} < \frac{g_b}{b}.
$$

*Proof.* All denominators are positive. Cross-multiplying, the first inequality is $(b-g_b)(a+b) < b\,(a+b-g_a-g_b)$, which simplifies to $b\,g_a < a\,g_b$; dividing by $ab>0$ gives the second. $\square$

Combined with Theorem 3.6, the per-block gains are $g = \|D^{-1}B^\top u\|_D^2$ for the respective blocks, so the tail share falls precisely when the tail's errors are proportionally better correlated with their free weights.

## 5. The experiment

### 5.1 Protocol

* **Model:** Qwen2.5-0.5B (24 transformer layers), evaluation context 512 tokens.
* **Metric:** $\Delta\mathrm{CE}$, the increase of next-token cross-entropy over the unquantized model, and *retained accuracy*, the ratio of quantized to unquantized next-token accuracy. The unquantized baseline (accuracy $0.4460$, cross-entropy $2.8697$) was reproduced exactly before any arm was run.
* **GPTQ implementation:** sequential layer-wise processing, with inputs to each layer recaptured from the already-quantized prefix of the network; curvature accumulated by hooks on the actual linear modules; quantization blocks aligned to groups of 128; Cholesky factorization of the damped inverse curvature, retried with escalating damping on failure (schedule fixed before the run). Calibration: 16 sequences drawn from the training side only. No column reordering ("act-order").
* **Reference floors** (from the preceding round, same harness): per-channel 4-bit RTN $+0.788$; grouped 4-bit RTN $+0.318$; per-channel 6-bit RTN $+0.035$; per-channel 3-bit RTN $+9.23$; grouped 3-bit RTN $+2.72$.

### 5.2 Results

| Arm | $\Delta\mathrm{CE}$ | retained accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| GPTQ 4-bit $g{=}128$, all layers | $+0.1512$ | $0.9546$ |
| GPTQ 4-bit $g{=}128$, core (layers 0–21) | $+0.1235$ | $0.9641$ |
| GPTQ 3-bit $g{=}128$, all layers | $+1.1932$ | $0.7086$ |

The full ladder:

| bits | per-channel RTN | grouped RTN | grouped GPTQ | grouping lever | compensation lever | compounded |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | $0.788$ | $0.318$ | $0.1512$ | $2.478$ | $2.103$ | $5.212$ |
| 3 | $9.23$ | $2.72$ | $1.1932$ | $3.393$ | $2.280$ | $7.736$ |

### 5.3 Pre-registered predictions, assessed in exact arithmetic

* **P1** ($\Delta\mathrm{CE}\le 0.15$ for GPTQ 4-bit): **missed.** $0.1512 - 0.15 = 0.0012 > 0$. (The run's own log described this as confirmed "at the boundary"; the exact comparison does not support that reading. The substantive finding — a $2.10\times$ improvement over grouped RTN — stands.)
* **P2** ($\Delta\mathrm{CE}\le 0.14$, approaching the 6-bit per-channel floor): **refuted.**
* **P3** (the final two layers contribute more than $25\%$ of the compensated loss): **refuted.** The tail increment is exactly $0.1512 - 0.1235 = 0.0277$, and the share $0.0277/0.1512 \approx 0.1832$ lies strictly between $1/6$ and $1/5$.

### 5.4 Deployment table (6 GB host)

| scheme | usable at | cost |
|---|---|---|
| per-channel RTN | $\ge 6$ bits | $+0.035$ at 6 bits; $+0.788$ at 4 bits |
| grouped RTN | 4 bits | $+0.32$ |
| grouped GPTQ | 4 bits (3 bits survivable) | $+0.15$ (3 bits: $+1.19$) |

### 5.5 Engineering hazards

Three silent errors were caught before the reported runs: (1) hooks registered on container modules rather than linear modules, detected by checking the width of captured activations; (2) a broadcasting error in per-column scales; (3) loss of numerical positive definiteness of the curvature computed from partially quantized activations, handled by escalating damping. A single-matrix regression test is retained: on one random layer, GPTQ must beat RTN on layer-output error. Corollary 3.7 guarantees that each compensation step cannot hurt *for the error it corrects*; since compensation also changes the weights rounded later, and hence their rounding errors, the end-to-end comparison is an empirical check rather than a theorem.

## 6. Theory meets data

**Proposition 6.1 (Exact ladder facts).** In exact rational arithmetic:

1. $0.1512 > 0.15$, with difference $0.0012$.
2. The tail increment is $0.0277$ and $1/6 < 0.0277/0.1512 < 1/5$.
3. The 4-bit compensation lever satisfies $2.1 \le 0.318/0.1512 < 2.11$.
4. The compensation lever drifts by less than $9\%$: $1 < \dfrac{2.72/1.1932}{0.318/0.1512} < 1.09$.
5. The grouping lever drifts by more than $35\%$: $\dfrac{9.23/2.72}{0.788/0.318} > 1.35$.
6. The compounded lever exceeds $5$ at 4 bits and $7.7$ at 3 bits.

*Proof.* Direct computation with the rational values. $\square$

**Theorem 6.2 (No single rescaled quadratic model).** There are no matrices $A,B,D$ (with $D$ invertible), error vector $u$, and scalar $t\ne0$ such that simultaneously

$$
q_A(u) = 0.318,\quad q_S(u) = 0.1512,\quad q_A(tu) = 2.72,\quad q_S(tu) = 1.1932 .
$$

*Proof.* By Theorem 3.10 the ratios $q_S/q_A$ at $u$ and at $tu$ coincide, but $0.1512/0.318 \neq 1.1932/2.72$ (cross-multiplying: $0.1512\cdot 2.72 = 0.411264 \ne 0.379437\ldots = 1.1932\cdot 0.318$). $\square$

*Interpretation.* Within the quadratic model, the $8.4\%$ drift of the compensation lever cannot be a scale effect. It must reflect a change of error **shape** between bit widths — the pattern of rounding directions, and in particular clipping at group extremes — or a departure of the true loss from its quadratic approximation. The much larger drift of the grouping lever is consistent with grouping being intrinsically a shape-changing operation: it removes outlier-driven grid stretching, whose damage grows as the grid coarsens.

**Reading the tail share.** By Theorem 4.6, the observed $18\%$ compensated tail share is smaller than the RTN tail share if and only if compensation's relative gain in layers 22–23 exceeds that in layers 0–21. The RTN core-only arm, a single cheap run, would decide this.

## 7. Algorithms

**Algorithm 1 (Column-sequential GPTQ for one weight row).** Input: weights $w\in\mathbb{R}^d$, damped curvature $H_\lambda = H+\lambda I$, bit width $b$, group size $g$.

1. Compute $H_\lambda^{-1}$ and its upper Cholesky factor $U$ ($H_\lambda^{-1} = U^\top U$). On failure, increase $\lambda$ and retry.
2. For $q = 1,\dots,d$:
   1. If $q$ starts a group, fix the group's grid (scale and zero point) from the *current* weights $w_{q:q+g-1}$.
   2. $\hat w_q \leftarrow \mathrm{round}(w_q)$ on the group grid; $\varepsilon \leftarrow (w_q - \hat w_q)/U_{qq}$.
   3. $w_j \leftarrow w_j - \varepsilon\, U_{qj}$ for all $j>q$.
3. Return $\hat w$.

$U_{qq}^2$ equals the $(q,q)$ entry of the inverse of the trailing block $H_\lambda[q{:},q{:}]$, so step 2.2–2.3 is precisely the OBS update of Theorem 4.3 applied to the current free set $\{q+1,\dots,d\}$; summing these per-column costs reproduces the final loss (numerically exact in our demonstrations). The cost is $O(d^3)$ for the factorization plus $O(d^2)$ per row; the factorization is shared across all rows of a layer.

**Algorithm 2 (Fixed-protocol ladder).** For each bit width $b\in\{4,3\}$ and each arm (per-channel RTN, grouped RTN, grouped GPTQ), quantize all target linear modules with the same reference model, calibration data, evaluation set and grouping, and report $\Delta\mathrm{CE}$ and retained accuracy; compute grouping, compensation and compounded levers as ratios of successive floors.

## 8. Discussion

**What the theory says.** Compensation is exactly the elimination of the free weights from a quadratic form. Its floor is the Schur complement, reached by a unique linear correction; its gain is a $D$-energy that vanishes iff the error is uncorrelated with the free weights. The ubiquity of the Schur complement explains the success of GPTQ without appeal to any specific property of language models beyond correlated activations.

**What the data say.** On a real 0.5B model, the compensation lever is about $2.1$–$2.3\times$, compounding with grouping to more than $5\times$ (4 bits) and $7.7\times$ (3 bits). The last two layers remain measurably more expensive, but compensation compresses their share.

**Limitations.** The guarantees of Sections 3–4 concern a fixed error vector; in sequential quantization the later rounding errors depend on earlier updates, so the end-to-end superiority of GPTQ over RTN is empirical (it held in every measured arm). One model; context 512; no act-order; 16 calibration sequences; the quadratic model is a local surrogate for cross-entropy, so theorems about $q_H$ constrain the data only through that surrogate. Theorem 6.2 is a statement about the quadratic model: it shows the measured pairs cannot be explained by error rescaling within it, not that cross-entropy is or is not quadratic.

## 9. Future work

1. **Correlation-spectrum law.** Conjecture: under independent uniform rounding errors, the expected GPTQ/RTN ratio for a layer is $\operatorname{tr}\big(\operatorname{diag}(H^{-1})^{-1}\big)/\operatorname{tr}(H)$ up to sequential-order corrections, so the lever is predictable from the curvature alone (Theorem 4.3 gives the per-column compensated cost $\mathbb{E}[e^2]/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$ against the RTN cost $\mathbb{E}[e^2]H_{qq}$).
2. **Sequential telescoping and act-order.** Conjecture: the total loss of column-sequential GPTQ equals $\sum_q e_q^2/d_q$ with $d_q$ the successive pivots (via the Crabtree–Haynsworth quotient property of iterated Schur complements), and processing columns by descending $H_{qq}$ minimizes the worst-case bound $\sum_q (s_q^2/4)/d_q$, with $s_q$ the grid step.
3. **Tail-share compression.** If tail errors are relatively better correlated with free weights, the RTN tail share at 4 bits should exceed $18\%$; one RTN core-only run tests this via Theorem 4.6.
4. **Shape-drift decomposition.** The 4→3-bit lever drift $2.103\to2.280$ should be explained by the change of normalized error direction $u/\|u\|$ and may vanish after re-scaling 3-bit errors by grouped clipping statistics.
5. **Engineering:** act-order variant, a joint weight + KV-cache budget optimizer, tail-aware mixed precision keeping layers 22–23 at higher bit width, and transfer to Qwen2.5-1.5B.

## 10. Conclusion

A century-old identity — completing the square in block form — fully accounts for the mechanics of compensated quantization: the unavoidable cost is a Schur complement, the avoidable cost is removed by a unique update, and the gain is strict exactly when errors and free weights are correlated. On a real 0.5B model, this mechanism halves the damage of grouped rounding at 4 bits and makes 3-bit weights survivable, while the residual drift of its lever tells us that coarser grids change the *shape* of the rounding error, not merely its size.

\section{Introduction}

Running a modern language model on commodity hardware---our reference target is a host with 6\,GB of
memory---requires compressing its weights well below 16 bits. The simplest scheme, round-to-nearest onto a
uniform grid, degrades quickly as the bit width drops. Two structural levers are commonly used to improve it:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Grouping}: instead of one grid (scale and zero point) per output channel, use one grid per
contiguous group of $g$ input weights (here $g=128$), so that outliers only stretch the grid of their own group.
\item \emph{Compensation}: quantize weights sequentially and, after each rounding decision, update the
not-yet-quantized weights to cancel the induced change in the layer output as well as possible. This is the
GPTQ algorithm of Frantar, Ashkboos, Hoefler and Alistarh~\cite{gptq}, a scalable descendant of the Optimal
Brain Surgeon (OBS) of Hassibi and Stork~\cite{obs}.
\end{enumerate}
Neither lever is new. The contributions of this paper are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{A fixed-protocol ladder.} All arms---per-channel RTN, grouped RTN and grouped GPTQ, at 4 and 3
bits---are measured on one validated harness with a shared reference, protocol and granularity (Section~\ref{sec:exp}).
\item \textbf{A tail-share quantification.} The last two transformer layers contribute $18\%$ of the
compensated loss.
\item \textbf{A complete structural explanation of compensation} in the quadratic model, phrased entirely
through the Schur complement (Sections~\ref{sec:setting}--\ref{sec:gptq}).
\item \textbf{A falsification bridge} between theory and data: the measured drift of the compensation lever
certifies that the error shape changes between bit widths (Section~\ref{sec:bridge}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Setting and definitions}\label{sec:setting}

All matrices are real. For a symmetric matrix $M$ and a vector $x$ write $q_M(x)=x^\top Mx$.

\begin{definition}[Layer-wise quadratic loss]
Let a linear layer with weight row $w\in\R^d$ be evaluated on calibration inputs $x_1,\dots,x_N\in\R^d$.
The \emph{curvature} is $H=\frac1N\sum_k x_kx_k^\top$ (in practice plus a small damping $\lambda I$).
Perturbing the weights by $\delta$ changes the outputs by $\delta^\top x_k$, and the mean squared output
change is $L(\delta)=q_H(\delta)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Quantized/free split]
Partition the coordinates into a \emph{quantized} set $Q$ ($|Q|=m$) and a \emph{free} set $F$ ($|F|=n$), and write
\[
H=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\ B^\top&D\end{pmatrix},\qquad A\in\R^{m\times m},\ B\in\R^{m\times n},\ D\in\R^{n\times n},
\]
with $\delta=(u,v)$, where $u\in\R^m$ is the rounding error on $Q$ (fixed once rounding is done) and
$v\in\R^n$ is the update applied to the free weights (to be chosen). We always assume $D$ positive definite.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Schur complement and optimal update]
$S=A-BD^{-1}B^\top$ and $v^\star(u)=-D^{-1}B^\top u$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[RTN loss, compensated loss, lever]
The \emph{RTN loss} of $u$ is $L(u,0)=q_A(u)$; the \emph{compensated loss} is $\min_vL(u,v)$; the
\emph{compensation lever} is the ratio of the RTN loss to the compensated loss.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$D$-norm]
For $D$ positive definite, $\|z\|_D^2=z^\top Dz\ge0$, with equality only for $z=0$.
\end{definition}

\section{Compensation as a Schur complement}\label{sec:schur}

\begin{theorem}[OBS split]\label{thm:split}
For all $u\in\R^m$ and $v\in\R^n$,
\[
L(u,v)=\bigl\|D^{-1}B^\top u+v\bigr\|_D^2+u^\top S\,u .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Expand $L(u,v)=u^\top Au+2u^\top Bv+v^\top Dv$. With $z=D^{-1}B^\top u$, the right-hand side is
$z^\top Dz+2z^\top Dv+v^\top Dv+u^\top Au-u^\top BD^{-1}B^\top u$. Since $z^\top Dz=u^\top BD^{-1}B^\top u$
and $z^\top Dv=u^\top Bv$ (by symmetry of $D^{-1}$), the two expressions coincide.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[RTN sees only the quantized block]\label{lem:rtn}
$L(u,0)=q_A(u)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Immediate from the block expansion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[OBS lower bound]\label{thm:lower}
For every update $v$, $u^\top Su\le L(u,v)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first summand in Theorem~\ref{thm:split} is a $D$-norm, hence non-negative.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Attainment]\label{thm:attain}
$L(u,v^\star(u))=u^\top Su$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
With $v=v^\star(u)$ the vector inside the $D$-norm vanishes.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness]\label{thm:unique}
$L(u,v)=u^\top Su$ if and only if $v=v^\star(u)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:split}, equality holds iff $\|D^{-1}B^\top u+v\|_D^2=0$, iff $D^{-1}B^\top u+v=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact compensation gain]\label{thm:gain}
$q_A(u)-q_S(u)=\bigl\|D^{-1}B^\top u\bigr\|_D^2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:split} at $v=0$ and use Lemma~\ref{lem:rtn}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Compensation never hurts]\label{cor:never}
$q_S(u)\le q_A(u)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Strictness criterion]\label{thm:strict}
$q_S(u)<q_A(u)$ if and only if $B^\top u\neq0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:gain} the gain is positive iff $D^{-1}B^\top u\neq0$, and since $D$ is invertible this
holds iff $B^\top u\neq0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Compensation strictly helps exactly when the rounding error is correlated, through the cross-curvature $B$,
with the weights still free to move.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Non-negativity]
If $H$ is positive semidefinite, then $q_S(u)\ge0$ for all $u$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$q_S(u)=L(u,v^\star(u))=q_H\bigl((u,v^\star(u))\bigr)\ge0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:attain}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Scale invariance of the lever]\label{thm:scale}
For every $t\neq0$, $\dfrac{q_S(tu)}{q_A(tu)}=\dfrac{q_S(u)}{q_A(u)}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$q_M(tu)=t^2q_M(u)$ for every $M$; cancel $t^2\neq0$.
\end{proof}

\section{The GPTQ column formula and structural consequences}\label{sec:gptq}

\begin{theorem}[Block inverse]\label{thm:blockinv}
If $H$ is invertible and $D$ is positive definite, the $Q\times Q$ block of $H^{-1}$ equals $S^{-1}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By the classical block-inversion formula,
\[
H^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}S^{-1}&-S^{-1}BD^{-1}\\ -D^{-1}B^\top S^{-1}&D^{-1}+D^{-1}B^\top S^{-1}BD^{-1}\end{pmatrix},
\]
which is verified by direct multiplication.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:pd}
If $H$ is positive definite, so is $D$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $x\neq0$, $x^\top Dx=(0,x)^\top H(0,x)>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[GPTQ / OBS column cost]\label{thm:column}
Let $H$ be positive definite, let $Q=\{q\}$ be a single coordinate quantized with rounding error $e\in\R$,
and let all other coordinates be free. Then
\[
L\bigl(e,v^\star(e)\bigr)=\frac{e^2}{[H^{-1}]_{qq}} .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:attain} the loss is $Se^2$ with $S$ a scalar, and $S=q_H\bigl((1,v^\star(1))\bigr)>0$.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:blockinv}, $[H^{-1}]_{qq}=S^{-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Diagonal inequality]\label{cor:diag}
For every positive definite $H$ and every index $q$, $H_{qq}\,[H^{-1}]_{qq}\ge1$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
For $e=1$ the RTN cost is $H_{qq}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:rtn}) and the compensated cost is $1/[H^{-1}]_{qq}$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:column}). By Corollary~\ref{cor:never}, $1/[H^{-1}]_{qq}\le H_{qq}$; multiply by
$[H^{-1}]_{qq}>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Wider windows never hurt]\label{thm:window}
Split $F=F_1\sqcup F_2$ and let $S_1$ be the Schur complement computed with $F_1$ alone as free set. Then
$q_S(u)\le q_{S_1}(u)$ for all $u$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The $F_1\times F_1$ block of $D$ is positive definite (Lemma~\ref{lem:pd}). Freezing the $F_2$ weights at
zero reduces the full loss $L(u,(v_1,0))$ to the restricted loss of $(u,v_1)$. At the restricted optimum,
$q_{S_1}(u)$ is a value of the full loss, hence at least $q_S(u)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:lower}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tail-share criterion]\label{thm:tail}
Let core and tail blocks have RTN costs $a,b>0$ and compensation gains $g_a<a$, $g_b<b$. Then
\[
\frac{b-g_b}{(a-g_a)+(b-g_b)}<\frac{b}{a+b}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{g_a}{a}<\frac{g_b}{b}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
All denominators are positive. Cross-multiplying, the left inequality reads
$(b-g_b)(a+b)<b(a+b-g_a-g_b)$, i.e.\ $bg_a<ag_b$; divide by $ab>0$.
\end{proof}

\section{The experiment}\label{sec:exp}

\paragraph{Protocol.} Qwen2.5-0.5B (24 transformer layers), context 512. Metric: $\DCE$ (increase of
next-token cross-entropy) and retained accuracy (quantized over unquantized next-token accuracy). The
unquantized baseline (accuracy $0.4460$, cross-entropy $2.8697$) was reproduced exactly. GPTQ: sequential
layer-wise processing with inputs recaptured from the already-quantized prefix; curvature accumulated on the
actual linear modules; blocks aligned to groups of 128; Cholesky factorization of the damped inverse
curvature with an escalating-damping retry schedule fixed before the run; 16 calibration sequences from the
training side only; no column reordering. Reference floors on the same harness: per-channel RTN $+0.788$
(4 bits), $+9.23$ (3 bits), $+0.035$ (6 bits); grouped RTN $+0.318$ (4 bits), $+2.72$ (3 bits).

\paragraph{Pre-registered predictions.}
\textbf{P1} ($\DCE\le0.15$ at 4 bits): missed, since $0.1512-0.15=0.0012>0$; the substantive $2.10\times$
improvement over grouped RTN stands. \textbf{P2} ($\DCE\le0.14$): refuted. \textbf{P3} (tail share
$>25\%$): refuted; the tail increment is $0.0277$ and $1/6<0.0277/0.1512\approx0.1832<1/5$.

\paragraph{Deployment (6\,GB host).} Per-channel RTN is unusable below 6 bits; grouped RTN is viable at 4
bits ($+0.32$); grouped GPTQ is viable at 4 bits ($+0.15$) and survivable at 3 bits ($+1.19$).

\paragraph{Engineering hazards.} Hooks on container instead of linear modules (caught by activation-width
checks), column-scale broadcasting, and loss of numerical positive definiteness under partially quantized
activations (handled by escalating damping). A single-matrix regression test requires GPTQ to beat RTN on
layer-output error. Corollary~\ref{cor:never} guarantees that each compensation step cannot hurt for the error it corrects; because compensation also changes the weights rounded later, the end-to-end comparison is an empirical check rather than a theorem.

\section{Theory meets data}\label{sec:bridge}

\begin{proposition}[Exact ladder facts]
In exact rational arithmetic: (1) $0.1512>0.15$ with difference $0.0012$; (2) the tail increment is
$0.0277$ and $1/6<0.0277/0.1512<1/5$; (3) $2.1\le0.318/0.1512<2.11$; (4)
$1<\frac{2.72/1.1932}{0.318/0.1512}<1.09$; (5) $\frac{9.23/2.72}{0.788/0.318}>1.35$; (6)
$0.788/0.1512>5$ and $9.23/1.1932>7.7$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Direct computation.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No single rescaled quadratic model]\label{thm:nomodel}
There are no $A,B,D$ (with $D$ invertible), $u$ and $t\neq0$ such that $q_A(u)=0.318$, $q_S(u)=0.1512$,
$q_A(tu)=2.72$ and $q_S(tu)=1.1932$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:scale} the ratios at $u$ and $tu$ would coincide, but
$0.1512\cdot2.72=0.411264\neq0.3794376=1.1932\cdot0.318$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Within the quadratic model, the $8.4\%$ drift of the compensation lever is therefore not a scale effect: it
reflects a change of error shape (rounding directions, clipping at group extremes) or a departure from
quadratic behaviour. The much larger drift of the grouping lever is consistent with grouping being a
shape-changing operation. By Theorem~\ref{thm:tail}, the $18\%$ compensated tail share is below the RTN
tail share iff compensation's relative gain in layers 22--23 exceeds that in layers 0--21.
\end{remark}

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithm}[Column-sequential GPTQ for one row]
Input $w\in\R^d$, damped curvature $H_\lambda=H+\lambda I$, bits $b$, group size $g$.
(1) Compute the upper Cholesky factor $U$ of $H_\lambda^{-1}=U^\top U$, increasing $\lambda$ on failure.
(2) For $q=1,\dots,d$: if $q$ starts a group, fix its grid from the current weights $w_{q:q+g-1}$; set
$\hat w_q=\mathrm{round}(w_q)$, $\varepsilon=(w_q-\hat w_q)/U_{qq}$, and $w_j\leftarrow w_j-\varepsilon U_{qj}$
for $j>q$. (3) Return $\hat w$.
\end{algorithm}
Here $U_{qq}^2$ is the $(q,q)$ entry of the inverse of the trailing block $H_\lambda[q{:},q{:}]$, so each
step is the OBS update of Theorem~\ref{thm:column} on the current free set. Cost: $O(d^3)$ for the shared
factorization plus $O(d^2)$ per row.

\begin{algorithm}[Fixed-protocol ladder]
For each $b\in\{4,3\}$ and each arm (per-channel RTN, grouped RTN, grouped GPTQ), quantize all target linear
modules with the same reference model, calibration data, evaluation set and grouping; report $\DCE$ and
retained accuracy; compute levers as ratios of successive floors.
\end{algorithm}

\section{Discussion and limitations}

Compensation is exactly the elimination of the free weights from a quadratic form: its floor is a Schur
complement, reached by a unique linear correction, and its gain is a $D$-energy that vanishes iff the error is
uncorrelated with the free weights. On a real 0.5B model the compensation lever is $2.1$--$2.3\times$,
compounding with grouping to more than $5\times$ (4 bits) and $7.7\times$ (3 bits). Limitations: the guarantees of Sections~\ref{sec:schur}--\ref{sec:gptq} concern a fixed error vector, whereas in sequential quantization later rounding errors depend on earlier updates, so the end-to-end superiority of GPTQ over RTN is empirical (it held in every measured arm); one model;
context 512; no act-order; 16 calibration sequences; the quadratic model is a local surrogate for
cross-entropy, so Theorem~\ref{thm:nomodel} constrains the data only through that surrogate.

\section{Future work}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Correlation-spectrum law.} Conjecture: under independent uniform rounding errors, the expected
GPTQ/RTN ratio is $\tr\bigl(\diag(H^{-1})^{-1}\bigr)/\tr(H)$ up to sequential-order corrections.
\item \textbf{Sequential telescoping and act-order.} Conjecture: column-sequential GPTQ loss equals
$\sum_qe_q^2/d_q$ with $d_q$ the successive pivots (Crabtree--Haynsworth quotient property), and descending
$H_{qq}$ order minimizes the worst-case bound $\sum_q(s_q^2/4)/d_q$.
\item \textbf{Tail-share compression.} The RTN tail share at 4 bits should exceed $18\%$; one RTN core-only
run tests this via Theorem~\ref{thm:tail}.
\item \textbf{Shape-drift decomposition.} The lever drift $2.103\to2.280$ should be explained by the change of
$u/\|u\|$ and may vanish after re-scaling 3-bit errors by grouped clipping statistics.
\item \textbf{Engineering.} Act-order, a joint weight + KV-cache budget optimizer, tail-aware mixed precision
for layers 22--23, and transfer to Qwen2.5-1.5B.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}
Completing the square in block form fully accounts for the mechanics of compensated quantization: the
unavoidable cost is a Schur complement, the avoidable cost is removed by a unique update, and the gain is
strict exactly when errors and free weights are correlated. On a real 0.5B model this halves the damage of
grouped rounding at 4 bits and makes 3-bit weights survivable, while the residual drift of the lever shows
that coarser grids change the shape of the rounding error, not merely its size.
